oauthPkce.title: OAuth 2.0 authorization code and PKCE
oauthPkce.heading: OAuth 2.0 authorization code and PKCE
oauthPkce.lead: When a user wants an application to access their resources at another service, OAuth 2.0 lets the application obtain an access token from an authorization server. This example uses a server-side client and a browser to show the authorization code flow and how Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) binds the code to the request.
oauthPkce.footer: This example uses a server-side client and S256; endpoints and permissions depend on the provider. Continue with OIDC single sign-on and access and refresh tokens.
oauthPkce.overviewTitle: Overview: from user authorization to resource access
oauthPkce.overview:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|Operates| B[Browser]
    B -->|Start and callback| C[Client application]
    B -->|Login and consent| A[Authorization server]
    C -->|Code and verifier| A
    A -->|Access token| C
    C -->|Token and resource request| R[Resource server]
    R -->|Protected resource| C
oauthPkce.overviewNote: The browser carries the authorization request and callback; the client exchanges the code at the token endpoint and uses the access token to request resources.
oauthPkce.supplement:
How PKCE binds the code

For each request, the client generates a random code_verifier and calculates code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))) without padding. The authorization request sends only the challenge; the verifier is sent over HTTPS during exchange. The server recalculates and compares the challenge, preventing someone who intercepts only the code from redeeming it.

PKCE does not protect an access token that has already leaked or replace secure verifier storage, callback validation, or client protection.

Authorization and authentication boundaries

  • Scope: scope describes requested access; the authorization server determines what is granted and the resource server must still check permissions.
  • Client type: Public clients cannot reliably keep a client secret and must use PKCE. PKCE is also recommended for confidential clients, which still authenticate as required.
  • Callback protection: This example binds state to the user session to correlate the callback and prevent cross-site request forgery; the authorization server should strictly match registered redirect URIs.
  • Authentication: OAuth is an authorization framework; an access token should not itself be treated as proof of login to the client. For login, use OIDC and validate the ID token.

References: RFC 6749 · RFC 7636 · RFC 9700

sessionCookie.lead: The server stores login state and sends an opaque session identifier in Set-Cookie. The browser sends the cookie on matching requests, allowing the server to find the session.
sessionCookie.overview:
flowchart LR
 B[Browser] -->|Credentials| S[Server]
 S -->|Save session| D[(Session store)]
 S -->|Set-Cookie| B
 B -->|Later request with cookie| S
 S -->|Look up session| D
 S -->|Response| B
sessionCookie.overviewNote: The cookie carries an identifier; the server checks the session store for login state.
sessionCookie.extra: The session store holds login state; the cookie carries its identifier. HttpOnly prevents page scripts from reading the cookie, Secure limits transmission to HTTPS, and SameSite mitigates some cross-site request forgery scenarios.
sessionCookie.footer: This illustrates a common browser session cookie flow; behavior depends on the application.

accessSecretToken.lead: After authentication, a client may receive an access token for API calls and a longer-lived secret token for obtaining a new access token. In OAuth, the latter is usually called a refresh token.
accessSecretToken.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Client] -->|Login credentials| A[Authentication server]
 A -->|Access and refresh tokens| C
 C -->|Access token| B[Business server]
 B -->|Response| C
 C -.->|Refresh token when needed| A
accessSecretToken.overviewNote: The secret token in this example is a refresh token. Issuance and rotation depend on the system design.
accessSecretToken.extra: An access token is sent to the resource server, often in Authorization: Bearer. A refresh token is sent to the authentication server. A client secret identifies a confidential application and is a different credential.
accessSecretToken.footer: This is a general token login flow. Actual issuance, validation, and revocation depend on the system.

sso.lead: Single sign-on (SSO) lets an application delegate authentication to an external identity provider. The user authenticates through browser redirects, and the application creates its own session. Signing out of the application and the identity provider are separate operations. This example uses OpenID Connect (OIDC) authorization code flow with a server-side application.
sso.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[User] -->|Acts| B[Browser]
 B -->|Access and callback| A[Application]
 B -->|Authentication and optional logout| I[Identity provider]
 A -->|Exchange authorization code| I
 I -.->|Optional logout notification| A
sso.overviewNote: The browser follows redirects; the application and identity provider maintain separate sessions. The dashed line represents an optional notification when both sides support and configure it.
sso.supplement:
Sessions and logout scope

SessionPurposeEffect of logout
Application sessionIdentifies the user on later application requests.Ending it signs the user out of this application; the provider session may remain active.
Identity provider sessionRemembers authentication so other applications can reuse it.Ending it usually requires authentication again; existing application sessions do not necessarily end at the same time.

After local logout, an active provider session may allow the user to sign in again without entering credentials.

Integration and logout boundaries

  • Establish trust: Register the client and exact callback addresses, obtain endpoints and signing keys from trusted configuration, and use HTTPS throughout.
  • Protect the callback: Validate state, bind the authorization code with PKCE, and validate nonce when sent. Validate the ID token signature, issuer, audience, expiry and other applicable claims before creating a session.
  • Map accounts: Identify an external identity by its trusted issuer iss and subject sub. Account creation and linking are application policy; do not link solely on an unverified email address.
  • Logout propagation: Provider logout and notification of other applications are independent capabilities. Front-channel or back-channel notifications require support and configuration and can fail.
  • Token lifetime: Ending sessions does not necessarily revoke issued access tokens. Revoke tokens when needed and supported, and control their lifetimes.

References: OIDC Core · RP-initiated logout · Back-channel logout
sso.footer: This example uses a server-side OIDC application; provider capabilities and parameters vary. See OAuth 2.0 and PKCE and Session cookie login.

emailCode.lead: A user submits an email address and receives a one-time code. The server verifies the code and establishes a login session; possession of the code demonstrates current access to the mailbox.
emailCode.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[User] -->|Email and code| B[Browser or app]
 B -->|HTTPS requests| A[Authentication service]
 A -->|Store and verify code| R[(Code store)]
 A -->|Send email| M[Email provider]
 M -->|Deliver code| E[Mailbox]
 E -->|User reads code| U
 A -->|Create session| S[(Session store)]
 A -->|Session cookie| B
emailCode.overviewNote: The code is used for this authentication attempt; a new session maintains subsequent login state.
emailCode.extra: Use cryptographically secure random codes, short expirations, one-time consumption, and rate limits. Protect stored verification values, avoid account enumeration, and use HTTPS. Email codes depend on mailbox security and are not phishing-resistant multifactor authentication.
emailCode.footer: This example uses a session cookie; other systems may issue tokens.

threeDSecure.lead: 3D Secure (3DS) lets a merchant request cardholder authentication through the card network and issuing bank. The issuer assesses risk and may require a challenge. Payment authorization is a separate step.
threeDSecure.overview:
flowchart LR
 U[Cardholder] -->|Submit payment| M[Merchant or payment provider]
 M -->|3DS request| D[Directory server]
 D -->|Authentication request| A[Issuer authentication system]
 A -.->|Challenge when needed| U
 A -->|Authentication result| D
 D -->|Authentication result| M
 M -->|Payment authorization| P[Payment network]
 P -->|Authorization request| I[Issuer]
threeDSecure.overviewNote: The three domains are the acquirer, interoperability, and issuer domains. Deployments and roles vary.
threeDSecure.extra: Frictionless and challenge are possible authentication paths, not guarantees of success. Liability shift depends on network rules and transaction outcomes. 3DS does not prevent a user from being tricked into approving a fraudulent transaction.
threeDSecure.footer: This is a common 3DS flow; follow the applicable payment provider and card network requirements.

awsSts.lead: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues temporary credentials for an IAM role. This example uses cross-account AssumeRole: permission to assume a role and permission to access a resource are separate checks.
awsSts.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Caller] -->|AssumeRole| S[STS]
 S -->|Check trust and permissions| I[IAM policies]
 S -->|Temporary credentials| C
 C -->|Signed request and session token| R[AWS resource service]
 R -->|Authorized response| C
awsSts.overviewNote: This example uses a cross-account role; federation and AWS service credential paths differ.
awsSts.extra: Session policies can restrict role permissions but do not expand the role’s identity-based permissions. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and AssumeRoleWithSAML use different federation inputs. Explicit denies and other applicable policy limits still apply.
awsSts.footer: This example covers programmatic cross-account AssumeRole; other STS operations have different requirements.

awsIam.lead: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) helps control who can perform actions on AWS resources. This example follows a role session reading an Amazon S3 object in the same account.
awsIam.overview:
flowchart LR
 C[Caller] -->|Signed read request| S[S3 service]
 S -->|Authenticate and evaluate| P[IAM authorization]
 P -->|Allow or deny| S
 S -->|Read if allowed| R[(S3 object)]
 S -->|Result or error| C
awsIam.overviewNote: The caller already has temporary role credentials. IAM authorization here represents AWS evaluation, not a public IAM API call for every request.
awsIam.extra: Identity and resource policies can grant permissions. Permissions boundaries, session policies, and applicable organization policies can limit access; direct resource-policy grants to certain principals have special rules. Cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides. A role trust policy governs assumption of the role, while resource access is evaluated separately.
awsIam.footer: This is a simplified same-account request. See AWS STS for obtaining role credentials and AWS policy evaluation for details.
